issues.subcategory: Scope of sexual-behavior claim in opening rationale
issues.description: Scope of sexual-behavior claim in opening rationale: The claim about demonstrating uniqueness for “compulsive sexual behaviors” appears broader than the proposed sexual-behavior test can support. The design directly tests pornography use against gambling and substance-use domains, but it does not include other CSBD-relevant sexual behaviors, so any confirmed interaction would more securely support uniqueness for pornography-related self-perceived addiction than for compulsive sexual behaviors as a broader class.
issues.quote:
The present work aims to consider this possibility more thoroughly by examining how moral disapproval of a behavior interacts with frequency of the


behavior to predict self-perceived feelings of addiction. We propose to test these associations for pornography use and recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse), with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Design cannot establish uniqueness without testing gaming
issues.description: Design cannot establish uniqueness without testing gaming: The uniqueness claim is limited by the omission of gaming and internet-use domains, which the paper itself presents as motivating counterexamples in prior critiques. Null interactions for gambling and substances would show that moral incongruence does not generalize to those tested domains, but they would not by themselves establish uniqueness to sexual behavior relative to the very behavioral domains used to motivate the question.
issues.quote: We propose to test these associations for pornography use and recognized addictive disorders such as gambling and substance use disorders (i.e., alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, illicit substances, and prescription drug misuse), with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Overstrong psychopathology claim in Moral Incongruence
issues.description: Overstrong psychopathology claim in Moral Incongruence: The concluding claim that self-reported pornography addiction “likely reflects psychopathology” appears stronger than the evidence summarized in the paragraph supports. The cited findings establish clinical relevance and associations with distress, impairment, or reduced well-being, but several outcomes listed—such as relationship concerns, sexual satisfaction, and religious/spiritual functioning—do not by themselves show psychopathology.
issues.quote: Even when self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography are due to moral incongruence, it is likely that such feelings of dysregulation are clinically relevant. Cross-sectionally, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography is associated with greater psychological distress (Böthe et al., 2020; Grubbs et al., 2015, 2021), relationship concerns (Leonhardt et al., 2018), diminished sexual well-being (Vaillancourt-Morel et al., 2017), lower sexual satisfaction (Blais-Lecours et al., 2016; Böthe et al., 2021), and greater problems in religious and spiritual life (Wilt et al., 2016). Additionally, over time, greater self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography seems to predict greater psychological distress (Grubbs et al., 2015), greater future concerns about problematic use (Grubbs et al., 2018), and greater problems in religious and spiritual functioning (Grubbs et al., 2017). Moreover, moral incongruence regarding pornography use itself seems to predict greater experience of depression in men (Perry, 2018). In short, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography likely reflects psychopathology, regardless of whether or not such self-reports universally reflect dysregulated use.

issues.subcategory: Category error and contradiction in conceptualization
issues.description: Category error and contradiction in conceptualization: There seems to be an issue with the phrasing that early PPMI work “conceptualized moral incongruence as the direct effect” of moral disapproval. The intended contrast with the later interaction formulation is understandable, but this wording blurs the distinction between the construct of moral incongruence, its operationalization as moral disapproval among users, and the statistical association used to evaluate it.
issues.quote: Early work with the PPMI conceptualized moral incongruence as the direct effect of moral disapproval of pornography use on feelings of addiction to pornography among those that used pornography (Grubbs, Perry, et al., 2019; Grubbs \& Perry, 2019).

issues.subcategory: Conflating religiousness with moral disapproval
issues.description: Conflating religiousness with moral disapproval: The paragraph appears to overstate the direct evidence for moral disapproval as the moderator: after introducing studies on moral disapproval, two cited examples are described as using religiousness. Religiousness may be a proxy or antecedent of moral disapproval, and a later example does use moral disapproval directly, but the construct distinction matters for the refined interaction definition.
issues.quote: In support of the refined conception of moral incongruence, recent studies have demonstrated that moral disapproval of pornography does indeed moderate associations between use and self-reported addiction. In a representative sample of adults in the United States, religiousness moderated the relationship between pornography use and self-reported feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: Causal force overstated in PPMI claim
issues.description: Causal force overstated in PPMI claim: The phrase “clear contributor” may read as causal or etiological, whereas the cited evidence and the planned cross-sectional analyses more directly support statistical prediction by moral incongruence. The surrounding text often uses “predicts,” but this sentence could overstate what confirmed hypotheses would establish.
issues.quote: Ultimately, the PPMI model implies two strong claims regarding the role of moral incongruence in predicting self-perceived feelings of addiction. The first of these claims is relatively straightforward: moral incongruence is a clear contributor to self-reported feelings of addiction to, compulsivity in, or problems with pornography use. More simply, moral incongruence predicts feeling out of control in one's pornography use. The literature reviewed above robustly supports this claim.

issues.subcategory: Illogical support for the claim of uniqueness
issues.description: Illogical support for the claim of uniqueness: The support for the uniqueness claim does not fully follow as phrased. As described here, the cited literature establishes the importance of moral incongruence or religious conservatism for sexual-behavior problems, but uniqueness relative to gambling or substance use would require comparative evidence. The paragraph partly mitigates this by invoking the ICD-11 caveat and later critiques, but this sentence may overstate what the cited literature supports.
issues.quote: The claim is that the relationship between moral incongruence and self-reported feelings of addiction, compulsivity, or dysregulation is unique to sexual behaviors, particularly pornography use. This general observation is based on past literature that has consistently noted that religiously conservative individuals are especially likely to report experiencing problems with compulsive or addictive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent operationalization in The Present Study
issues.description: Inconsistent operationalization in The Present Study: The operationalization of moral incongruence is inconsistent at this point: the sentence defines it as moral disapproval $\times$ severity of consequences, whereas the preceding definition, the next sentence, the hypotheses, and the analytic plan define it as moral disapproval $\times$ behavioral frequency. Because consequence severity is outcome-like in the planned measures, this sentence could misstate the focal interaction even if the surrounding text indicates the intended model.
issues.quote: To accomplish this goal, we propose making use of an upcoming, nationally representative study of addictions in the U.S. population, which we describe in more detail in our methods section. Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action. That is, the present study seeks to test whether the observed effects of interactions present in prior literature for pornography use (i.e., between moral disapproval and frequency of use) extend to addictive disorders more broadly.

issues.subcategory: Implications section overextends from pornography to CSBD
issues.description: Implications section overextends from pornography to CSBD: The implications paragraph appears to overgeneralize from pornography-specific outcomes to sexual behaviors and CSBD more broadly. Because the planned sexual-behavior outcome is self-reported problematic pornography use, confirmed results would directly support the PPMI model for pornography and would bear on CSBD debates only indirectly; they would not demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behaviors as a class or directly corroborate the ICD-11 diagnostic caveat for CSBD. Furthermore, the hypotheses also predict positive direct effects of moral disapproval for gambling and substance problems, so the theoretical framing should distinguish why those nonsexual moral-disapproval effects would not raise analogous concerns about moral distress influencing self-reported dysregulation.
issues.quote: Should results confirm the above hypotheses, this work would have broad implications for current controversies regarding CSBD. Chiefly, should we find that moral incongruence-defined as the interaction between moral disapproval of a behavior and the frequency of engaging in that behavior-only predicts self-reported problematic use of pornography, then this work would provide strong evidence for the validity of the PPMI as a unique model for understanding self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography. Furthermore, should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD. Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of interaction effects with moral bias
issues.description: Conflation of interaction effects with moral bias: The implications language should more clearly separate interaction-defined moral incongruence from the direct effect of moral disapproval. Because the hypotheses anticipate positive moral-disapproval main effects for gambling and substance use, confirming them would still indicate that participant morality is associated with self-reported problems after accounting for frequency. That would not by itself prove diagnostic bias or show that caveats are needed for other disorders, but it complicates statements suggesting that only cross-domain interaction effects would imply systematic bias by morality.
issues.quote: Furthermore, should hypotheses be confirmed, there would be additional evidence supporting the inclusion of moral distress as a diagnostic consideration in the ICD-11 for CSBD. Demonstrating that moral incongruence appears to only be relevant in predicting feelings of dysregulation for sexual behaviors would corroborate the importance of CSBD being the only disorder to include a consideration about moral distress.

issues.subcategory: Sampling frame unclear in Participants and Procedure
issues.description: Sampling frame unclear in Participants and Procedure: The sampling frame and estimand for the main models are under-specified. The paper combines a 2,500-person sample matched to U.S. age and gender norms with a 1,500-person sports-wagering oversample, but the analytic plan does not state whether primary estimates will be weighted, stratified, adjusted for sample source, or restricted to the representative subset for population-level claims. This ambiguity affects claims in "The Present Study" section, specifically regarding gambling outcomes. Because the oversample is selected on a focal behavior, pooled unweighted models may estimate associations for the designed sample rather than for U.S. adults; this is especially relevant for the gambling moderation and equivalence tests, and potentially for substance-use models if sports wagerers differ systematically from the representative subset. Furthermore, Table 2 appears to apply general-population prevalence estimates to the full combined sample for non-gambling behaviors, while the gambling row separately accounts for the oversample. The power table should align with the intended analytic target—unweighted enriched-sample inference, weighted population inference, or another stated approach—because oversampling may affect both effective Ns and interpretation.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms. Due to the budgetary constraints associated with the larger grant funding effort from which this project is derived, the target sample size will be 2,500 American adults that match nationally representative norms for age and gender. Furthermore, due to the design of the larger project from which this sample is taken, we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: Substance Use: alcohol frequency may not index risk
issues.description: Substance Use: alcohol frequency may not index risk: The alcohol frequency predictor may be less aligned with alcohol-problem risk than the heavy-drinking frequency item that the NIDA Quick Screen uses. Because frequency of any drinking does not distinguish light regular drinking from episodic heavy drinking, alcohol-specific moderation or equivalence results could partly reflect this measurement choice rather than the absence or presence of moral incongruence for problematic alcohol use.
issues.quote: Beginning with the NIDA Quick Screen, we will assess past year frequency of alcohol use, nicotine products, prescription drugs for non-medical reasons, and illegal drugs. In its original form, the NIDA Quick Screen asks men to report alcohol frequency in terms of how many days they have consumed five or more drinks in a day and women to report alcohol frequency in terms of days they have consumed four or more drinks per day. Although we will include these response options, for the sake of the present study, we will look at alcohol frequency more generally (i.e., asking participants how often they have consumed alcohol without specifying the quantity consumed).

issues.subcategory: Substance Use scoring: parallel ASSIST use is ambiguous
issues.description: Substance Use scoring: parallel ASSIST use is ambiguous: The modified NIDA-ASSIST scoring rule is ambiguous for gambling and pornography. The preceding paragraph says these behaviors are added to the NIDA-ASSIST for fully parallel measurement, but the averaging rule is written only for substances and its parenthetical list omits gambling and pornography. The protocol should specify whether the same five-item modified ASSIST composites will be computed for those behaviors, and how those composites relate to the BPS and PGSI outcomes.
issues.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST. Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use ("In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?", "In the past three months, how often has your use of or engagement in the following led to health, social, legal, or financial problems for you?", and "During the past 3 months, how often have you failed to do what was normally expected of you because of your use of or engagement in the following?") on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) for each of the above mentioned substances. Participants will also respond to two questions "Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?" and "Have you ever tried and failed to control, cut down or stop using or engaging in the following?" for each substance on 3 point scale ( $0=$ No, Never; $3=$ Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and $6=$ Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Substance Use measures: problematic-use composite is not psychometrically parallel
issues.description: Substance Use measures: problematic-use composite is not psychometrically parallel: The modified NIDA-ASSIST composite may need additional psychometric rationale. It averages past-three-month frequency items scored 0 to 5 with lifetime/recent concern and failed-control items scored 0, 3, or 6. Because this average is used as the substance-use outcome in equivalence tests, the protocol should make clear why this modified score is an interpretable and comparably sensitive severity index across substances.
issues.quote: To assess problematic or potentially addictive use of these substances, we will take the average of responses to problematic use questions present in the NIDA-ASSIST. Participants will respond to three frequency based questions that assess problematic use ("In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge to use or engage in the following?", "In the past three months, how often has your use of or engagement in the following led to health, social, legal, or financial problems for you?", and "During the past 3 months, how often have you failed to do what was normally expected of you because of your use of or engagement in the following?") on a scale of 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day) for each of the above mentioned substances. Participants will also respond to two questions "Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?" and "Have you ever tried and failed to control, cut down or stop using or engaging in the following?" for each substance on 3 point scale ( $0=$ No, Never; $3=$ Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and $6=$ Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Substance Use measures: unclear tobacco/nicotine target
issues.description: Substance Use measures: unclear tobacco/nicotine target: The parenthetical list appears to separate tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine, whereas the surrounding protocol and supplemental items generally use a single tobacco/nicotine category. This should be clarified so the registered outcomes specify whether nicotine-related products form one composite or separate tobacco and non-tobacco nicotine outcomes.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions "Has a friend or relative or anyone else ever expressed concern about your use of or engagement in the following?" and "Have you ever tried and failed to control, cut down or stop using or engaging in the following?" for each substance on 3 point scale ( $0=$ No, Never; $3=$ Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and $6=$ Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged for each substance of interest (i.e., alcohol, tobacco, non-tobacco nicotine, prescription drugs, illicit drugs, cannabis).

issues.subcategory: Inclusion criteria conflict with earlier skip logic
issues.description: Inclusion criteria conflict with earlier skip logic: The Data Screening paragraph appears inconsistent with the skip logic in the Measures section. The Measures section says only past-year users/viewers complete further problematic-use items (specifically mentioning this for Substance Use and Pornography Use measures), whereas this passage says problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. This contradiction affects survey flow and planned missingness. The statement that universal administration yields behavior-specific subsets does not follow unless analyses are restricted by behavior engagement or skip logic. Because the moderation models and power projections (which use prevalence-defined effective Ns in Table 2) appear to rely on behavior-specific user subsets, the protocol should make clear whether non-users receive problematic-use outcomes, are scored as zero, or are excluded from each analysis, as this changes the estimand.
issues.quote:
As this data will be obtained via YouGov Opinion Polling, certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards. Accordingly, we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be administered to all participants regardless of their engagement in the behavior. That is, we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample. Therefore, for each analysis, we anticipate having slightly different subsets of the total sample.

issues.subcategory: Variable scaling is unclear for moderation tests
issues.description: Variable scaling is unclear for moderation tests: The preprocessing for the moderation/equivalence tests is under-specified. The plan says ASSIST/religiousness variables will be standardized, focal predictors and moderators centered, and later that key variables will be entered in raw form before computing the product. Although centering would not change the fitted interaction test in a fully specified linear model, the protocol should specify whether the product term used for reporting and equivalence testing is based on centered, standardized, or raw variables. Since the SESOI is justified using standardized interaction estimates and the decision rule refers to the observed standardized effect, the protocol should clarify what transformation is used for the interaction coefficient tested for equivalence.
issues.quote:
Data will be provided by YouGov in SPSS format. Accordingly, SPSS will be used to transform the above-described ASSIST items and measures of religiousness into standardized variables. Scale scores for included measures will also be calculated in SPSS. Additionally, focal predictors (behavioral frequency measures) and moderators (moral disapproval questions) will be centered and their interaction term calculated. Key dependent variables are listed in Table 1. After these initial data-processing procedures, data will be imported into and analyzed using $R$ statistical software. Descriptive statistics for included measures, as well as measures of internal consistency for included scales (Cronbach's alpha and Omega total), will be calculated using the psych package (Revelle, 2014). Bivariate correlations will be conducted across all included measures and reported using Holm-adjusted test statistics using the psych package.

Prior to our primary analyses, assumptions of regression (i.e., linearity, independence of residuals, homoscedasticity of residuals, normality of residuals) will be tested for each of the eight proposed outcomes. Although Ordinary Least Squares techniques (such as the moderation analyses conducted by the Interactive application) in large sample sizes are often robust against some violations (Schmidt \& Finan, 2018), in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate. Should results of moderation analyses remain robust (i.e., sign and significance of interaction effects remain the same across analytic techniques), we will present OLS results and corresponding graphs in text, with supplemental analyses included as appendices/supplemental materials.

As a primary test of our key hypotheses, we will conduct moderation analyses using the Im function in the stats package for R statistical software, followed by equivalence tests using the reg.equiv.fd function (Alter \& Counsell, 2021). For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed.

issues.subcategory: Contradictory primary SESOI threshold
issues.description: Contradictory primary SESOI threshold: This sentence conflicts with the immediately following SESOI rationale. It specifies $\delta=.27$ for the equivalence region, whereas the next paragraph says the equivalence region is $\delta=|.11|$ and describes that as the especially small SESOI for the primary analyses. The .27 value is discussed elsewhere as a prior pornography interaction estimate, so the primary registered bound is ambiguous.
issues.quote: For moderation analyses, key variables will be entered in their raw form during data processing in SPSS, and their product will be computed. We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell \& Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of $\delta=.27$.

issues.subcategory: Power section may not support equivalence claims
issues.description: Power section may not support equivalence claims: The power section appears to document NHST power to detect incremental interaction effects (e.g., $f^2 = .015$), but the confirmatory claims for gambling and substances also require positive equivalence conclusions. It is not clear from this section whether the planned sample sizes provide adequate power/precision for the Anderson-Hauck equivalence tests themselves. Furthermore, the adjusted-equivalence paragraph uses power to detect a historical pornography-sized effect ($f^2 = .12$; $1-\beta=.983$) as support for the smaller-sample contingency, but the proposed inference is comparative/equivalence-like—whether the non-pornography interaction is below a benchmark. The section should justify the power or precision for that equivalence/non-inferiority inference directly, rather than relying on NHST detection power alone.
issues.quote: As such, using G*Power 3.1 (Faul et al., 2009), we conducted a power analysis to determine the sample size needed to reliably detect our smallest effect of interest ( $\mathrm{f} 2=.015$ ), a series of sensitivity analyses to determine the likely power our final sample sizes would have to detect the effect size associated with our SESOI and equivalence region defined above, and a series of estimated achieved power based. The results are summarized in Table 2 below. For regression models with 6 predictors (age, gender, religiousness, moral disapproval, frequency, and the interaction of frequency and disapproval), our sample will be adequately powered (obtained power $>.80$ ) to detect even very small effects (below our SESOI of f2 $=.015$ ) for pornography use, gambling, alcohol use, tobacco/nicotine use, and cannabis/THC.

issues.subcategory: Discrepancy in the number of target behaviors
issues.description: Discrepancy in the number of target behaviors: There appears to be an internal count discrepancy: the paragraph says there will be 8 moderation analyses for 8 target behaviors/variables, but the surrounding list and Tables 1–2 appear to identify 7 behavioral domains. The protocol should clarify whether an eighth analysis is planned, or whether one of the listed domains has multiple confirmatory outcomes. Table 1 appears to list both validated scales and modified NIDA-ASSIST outcomes for pornography and gambling, which might explain the discrepancy. The outcome hierarchy for the modified NIDA-ASSIST pornography and gambling scores should be made explicit, particularly for identifying the confirmatory tests, the equivalence tests, and any cross-domain comparisons.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling assessed using the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency operationalization is unclear
issues.description: Gambling frequency operationalization is unclear: The gambling-frequency operationalization is internally inconsistent: the Methods section first says gambling frequency will be assessed with a single item, but later says an average across gambling behaviors will be taken, while the supplement shows only one global row (“Gambled or placed bets at all”). Because no multiple gambling-behavior frequency items are described, it is unclear which gambling frequency variable will enter the moderation model. The predictor construction should be made consistent.
issues.quote:
[TABLE]
Gambling Frequency In the past 12 months, how often have you engaged in any gambling behavior: For the present item, please note that gambling refers to any recreational activity in which money or something of value is wagered, bet, or risked for the potential of winning more money. Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money, placing bets on esports, placing bets on traditional sporting events, playing cards for money, placing bets online. | Gambling Frequency In the past 12 months, how often have you engaged in any gambling behavior: For the present item, please note that gambling refers to any recreational activity in which money or something of value is wagered, bet, or risked for the potential of winning more money.

issues.subcategory: Discrepant response scales for key measures
issues.description: Discrepant response scales for key measures: Several scoring/range discrepancies appear between Methods and the supplemental materials. The PGSI and BPS anchors in the supplement use nonstandard numeric values relative to the described 0-to-3 and 0-to-2 scoring (specifically, the PGSI anchors are listed as 0, 2, 4, and 5, and the BPS anchors as 0, 2, and 4). Even though the BPS anchors are a linear rescaling of 0/1/2, the registered instrument should make the intended scoring unambiguous. Additionally, the pornography and gambling frequency items are shown as 0-to-5 in the Substance Use section and supplemental materials, while the corresponding Methods text describes 1-to-6 scales. The PGSI/BPS discrepancies are the most consequential because they affect outcome scoring; the frequency-scale discrepancy is likely a recoding/centering issue but should still be aligned, as it creates ambiguity for the use-gating threshold and comparisons with other domains.

{"overall": "These observations address the structural mapping between the theoretical claims and the preregistered analytic plan, with an eye toward solidifying the protocol for a Stage 1 evaluation.

**Testing the domain-specific uniqueness claim**

The paper repeatedly frames the central claim around whether moral incongruence is unique to pornography/sexual behavior, especially in the Abstract, the Present Study, and the discussion of implications for the ICD-11 CSBD caveat. The analytic plan currently proposes separate moderation models and equivalence tests for gambling and substance domains. Demonstrating a significant pornography interaction alongside equivalent-to-zero non-pornography interactions provides suggestive evidence, but this does not constitute a formal statistical test that the pornography interaction is meaningfully larger than or distinct from the others.

A prespecified decision rule for the uniqueness claim—such as direct statistical contrasts of interaction effects across domains or a pooled model incorporating domain $\times$ frequency $\times$ moral-disapproval terms—would securely anchor the confirmatory test. Explicit criteria for support, disconfirmation, and inconclusive evidence regarding this uniqueness claim will strengthen the central inference.

**Sample weighting and analytic denominators**

The Participants section combines a 2,500-person U.S. matched sample with a 1,500-person sports-wagering oversample. The analysis plan does not yet detail whether primary analyses will use the national sample exclusively, the combined sample, sampling weights, a sample-source covariate, or separate baseline estimates. Unweighted estimation on the combined pool will materially impact gambling prevalence, gambling severity, and covariate distributions, precluding accurate generalization to U.S.-adult associations.

Furthermore, there is a structural contradiction regarding the analytic denominators. The Measures sections state that only past-year users complete problematic-use items, whereas the Data Screening section notes that problematic-use and moral-disapproval measures will be administered to all participants regardless of engagement. Detailing exactly who enters each primary model, how nonusers or zero-frequency respondents are handled, how non-administered outcome items are scored, and the target population for each estimate will resolve these ambiguities.

**Outcome measure comparability and construct overlap**

Testing cross-domain uniqueness relies on comparing outcomes that capture parallel addiction-like experiences across pornography, gambling, and substances. The current protocol leverages the BPS for pornography, the PGSI for gambling, and modified ASSIST averages for substances. This introduces substantial variation in recall windows, response structures, and item content.

A critical risk is that the pornography and gambling scales include items conceptually overlapping with moral appraisal or self-condemnation. The BPS incorporates continued use despite guilt, and the PGSI includes guilt about gambling and perceived problem status. This overlap threatens to artificially inflate associations with the moral disapproval predictor in the exact domains being used to adjudicate the uniqueness claim. Furthermore, the modified ASSIST outcome averages items with misaligned response metrics, combining 0–5 frequency items with 0/3/6 categorical items without a clear justification for the resulting implicit weighting. Designating a primary parallel outcome set, or prespecifying sensitivity analyses that exclude moral-guilt/problem-appraisal items and harmonize the modified ASSIST scoring, would fortify the comparative design.

**Equivalence of the predictor construct across domains**

While the moral-disapproval items share a formally parallel structure, the underlying construct they capture shifts substantially across domains. "Pornography use," "gambling," and "drinking alcohol" represent broad, legal behaviors. In contrast, "prescription drugs for non-medical reasons" and "illegal/illicit drugs" inherently embed notions of deviance, illegality, or misuse within the evaluated behavior.

Notably, alcohol frequency captures general consumption even with the inclusion of separate heavy-drinking items, whereas illicit drugs and prescription misuse collapse heterogeneous behaviors carrying distinct legal, health, and moral weights. The interaction term therefore risks capturing sexual morality in one model, legal condemnation in another, and health-risk disapproval in a third. Establishing that the exact same moral-incongruence mechanism is being evaluated across these domains requires substantive justification given the shifting nature of what participants are morally evaluating.

**Prespecifying analytic decisions**

As a Registered Report, the document must eliminate consequential degrees of freedom prior to data observation. Several pivot points in the equivalence, moderation, and robustness plan remain open. The protocol alternates between raw and standardized predictors, reports the equivalence SESOI inconsistently as $\delta = .27$ and $\delta = |.11|$, and lacks precision on how standardized interaction coefficients will be computed for ordinal frequency scales and centered product terms.

The fallback strategy for underpowered low-prevalence substances redefines the equivalence region based on a pornography effect. While highly valuable as an exploratory or benchmarking step, this strategy overrides the preregistered null-equivalence claim. Finally, the protocol anticipates potential OLS assumption violations but indicates only that supplemental analyses will be executed "as appropriate."
